source_text:
καὶ οὐ
νόμον τηρεῖ· πέπαυται γάρ. πτωχὰ δὲ στοιχεῖα εἰπὼν οὐ κατηγόρησεν ὡς πονηρῶν, ἀλλ' ὡς πλουτίζειν μὴ δυναμένων καὶ ἀρκεῖν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. 302 Gal 4,12 Μὴ νομίσητε, φησίν, ὅτι ἄλλην τινὰ λύπην εἶχον πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐπιπλήττω· τῆς γὰρ ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος συνεχῶς αὐτὸν μεταβάλλειν ἀναγκάζει τοῦ λόγου τὸ εἶδος, καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐπιτιμᾶν, νῦν δὲ παρακαλεῖν, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν κατηγορεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ θρηνεῖν. ἐνταῦθα τοίνυν διδάσκει ὡς ἅπερ γράφει, διὰ φιλοστοργίαν γράφει–οὐδὲν γάρ, φησί, παρ' ὑμῶν ἠδίκημαι–, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν, ὅτι μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι. Gal 4,15– 18 Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς. ἢ οὕτως· τὸ τηρεῖν νόμον ἢ τὸ πίστει ζῆν; καὶ ἐπειδὴ εἶπεν ὅτι ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἵνα τὸ τέλειον αὐτοὶ ἔχωσι τῆς πίστεως μὴ τηροῦντες νόμον, ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἐπήγαγεν ὅτι ταῦτα λέγω οὐ φθονῶν αὐτοῖς· ὤφελον γὰρ κἀκεῖνοι τέλειοι ἦσαν τῇ πίστει κεχρημένοι, καὶ ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς. καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν τοιαῦτα πράττετε ἃ καὶ ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ, ἵνα πάντες ὑμᾶς μιμῶνται, καὶ μὴ ὅταν ἔλθω αἰδεσθέντες με τοιοῦτοι γίνεσθε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμοῦ μὴ παρόντος ἑαυτοὺς διορθοῦσθε. Gal 4,23–24 Νῦν τῷ ὀνόματι κατεχρήσατο, οὐ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ἀλληγορίας. ἡ γὰρ ἀλληγορία οὐ στοιχεῖ τοῖς ῥητοῖς, ἄλλα δέ τινα ἐμφαινόμενα ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὑφὴν τῶν νοημάτων ἀκολουθίας εἰσάγει, οἷόν ἐστι τὸ φιλησάτω με ἀπὸ φιλημάτων στόματος αὐτοῦ, τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων· ἐκεῖ γὰρ οὔτε φίλημα οὔτε θρὶξ οὔτε κοιλία οὐδὲ μηροὶ οὐδὲ ἕτερόν τι, ἀλλ' ἄλλα δι' ἄλλων εἰσάγεται, καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀλληγορίας εἶδος κύριον. ἐνταῦθα δὲ καὶ ἡ ἱστορία ὡμολόγηται, καὶ ὅτι τύπος ἐστὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀποδέδεικται. ἡ οὖν δι' ἔργων προφητεία ἀλληγορία νῦν ὠνόμασται. τῶν γὰρ προφητειῶν αἱ μέν εἰσι διὰ λόγων μόνον ὡς τὸ ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, αἱ δὲ δι' ἔργων μόνον ὡς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, αἱ δὲ καὶ δι' ἔργων καὶ διὰ λόγων ὡς τὸ πρὸς 303 Ἰερεμίαν ῥηθέν, τὸ λάβε περίζωμα καινὸν καὶ περίθου· εἶτα θάψον αὐτὸ παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην, καὶ ὡς διερρύη τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ διεβρώθη, λάβε αὐτό, φησίν, ἐκεῖθεν. ἕως γὰρ τούτου δι' ἔργων ἡ προφητεία, τὸ δὲ ἑξῆς καὶ διὰ λόγων· ὅτι οὕτως κἀγὼ τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ περιεθέμην καὶ οὕτως αὐτοῖς ἐβοήθησα, καὶ οὕτως αὐτοὺς εἰς Βαβυλῶνα ἀπάγω αἰχμαλώτους καὶ σαθρωθέντας καὶ φθαρέντας ἐκεῖθεν ἀναγάγω καὶ ἀποκαθιστῶ.
thought_title: The law has ceased; Paul's allegory is prophecy through deeds
orientation: Eusebius is commenting on Galatians 4, explaining that the law has ceased after grace, that Paul's rebukes come from love, and that what Paul calls allegory is really prophecy enacted through historical events.
pass_a_gloss: And he does not keep the law; for it has ceased. [Eusebius distinguishes hearing commandments, which justify, from bodily works of the law, which are toilsome and cannot save.] And having called them poor basic principles [στοιχεῖα, elemental spirits or elementary teachings, here equivalent to the law], he did not accuse them as evil, but as not able to enrich and to suffice for piety. Do not think, he says, that I had some other grief toward you and because of this I rebuke you; for the suffering of the pain continually forces him to change the form of the speech, and now to rebuke, now to exhort, and sometimes to accuse, sometimes to lament. Here then he teaches that what things he writes, he writes because of affection—for in nothing, he says, have I been wronged by you—, but also as a healing, because most of all I have been deemed worthy of the greatest honor. What then is the blessing? Instead of: no one. Or thus: to keep the law or to live by faith? And since he said that those men want not you to be zealous, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith while not keeping the law, but you yourselves to be zealous, he added that I say these things not envying them; for would that they also were perfect, having used faith, and it was unhindered for them to be emulated and for us to be imitated. And you therefore do such things as also make you emulated, so that all may imitate you, and not when I come, having been ashamed before me, you become such, but also when I am not present correct yourselves. Now he used the name, not the power of allegory. For allegory does not follow the literal words, but introduces certain other things made visible from the sequence of thoughts according to the texture, such as is: let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, the one in the Song of Songs; for there neither kiss nor hair nor belly nor thighs nor any other thing, but other things through other things are introduced, and this is the proper form of allegory. But here both the history is acknowledged, and that it is a type of what is to come has been demonstrated. Therefore the prophecy through deeds has now been named allegory. For of prophecies, some are through words only, as: behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb; some through deeds only, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert; some both through deeds and through words, as what was said to Jeremiah: take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates, and when it had rotted with time and had been eaten away, take it, he says, from there. For up to this point the prophecy is through deeds, but what follows also through words: that thus I also put on the sons of Israel and thus I helped them, and thus I lead them away to Babylon as captives, and having become rotten and corrupted, I bring them up from there and restore them.

choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'basic principles' for στοιχεῖα and renders πτωχά literally as 'poor' to preserve the economic metaphor of inability to enrich.
The perfect tense indicates a completed state; 'has ceased' preserves the force that the law is no longer in effect.
Renders the key distinction Eusebius draws between prophecy through words, through deeds, and through both; 'deeds' keeps the concrete enacted sense.

choices.english: it is a type of what is to come
choices.why: Preserves the technical term 'type' for τύπος, which Eusebius uses to show the historical events point forward.
rejected: a pattern of what is coming

choices.why: κύριον here means 'proper' or 'authoritative'; renders Eusebius's claim that the Song of Songs exemplifies allegory in its strict sense.

choices.english: for would that they also were perfect
choices.why: ὤφελον with the indicative expresses an unattainable wish; 'would that' preserves the optative force of Paul's wish.

pass_b_english: And he is not keeping the law, for it has ceased. When he called the basic principles poor, he did not accuse them as evil, but as unable to enrich and to suffice for piety. Paul says, "Do not suppose that I had some other grievance against you and for that reason I rebuke you." The depth of his anguish constantly forces him to change the form of his speech—now rebuking, now encouraging, now accusing, now lamenting. Here, then, he teaches that what he writes, he writes out of affection—for I have been wronged in nothing by you, he says—but also as a remedy, because I considered it most valuable. What then is the blessedness? It belongs to no one. Or rather: is it keeping the law or living by faith? And since he said that the circumcision party do not want to emulate you, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added: "I say these things not envying them." For would that they also were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing hindered them from emulating and imitating us. So you also do such things as make you worthy of emulation, so that all may imitate you—and not only when I come, being ashamed before me, do you become such, but even when I am absent, set yourselves right. Now he used the name, not the power, of allegory. For allegory does not follow the literal words, but introduces other things made manifest from the sequence of thoughts according to their texture—such as: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth (Song of Songs 1:2). For in allegorical interpretation of the Song, it is not literally a kiss, nor hair, nor belly, nor thighs, nor anything else, but other things are introduced through other things, and this is the proper form of allegory. Here, however, the history is acknowledged, and it has been demonstrated that it is a type of what is to come. So the prophecy through deeds has now been named allegory. For of prophecies, some are through words alone, such as: Behold, the virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14); some through deeds alone, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9); and some through both deeds and words, such as what was said to Jeremiah: Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates (Jeremiah 13:1–11). And when it had rotted with time and was eaten away, take it from there, he says. For up to this point the prophecy is through deeds, but what follows is also through words: that in this way I also put on the sons of Israel, and in this way I put them on, and in this way I led them captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and been corrupted there, I bring them up from there and restore them.

problems.quote: do not want you to emulate them
problems.why: Greek ζηλοῦν means ‘to be jealous/zealous’, not ‘to emulate’. The sense of envy is lost.
problems.fix: do not want you to be jealous of them

problems.quote: it would have been unhindered for them to be emulated and for us to be imitated
problems.source_quote: ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς
problems.why: Greek says ‘it was impossible for them to be jealous and to imitate us’; English reverses the negation.
problems.fix: it was impossible for them to be jealous and to imitate us

problems.quote: but rather they want to emulate you
problems.why: Greek says 'but themselves to emulate you' (i.e., they want you to emulate them), not 'they want to emulate you'. Agency reversed.
problems.fix: but that they themselves be emulated by you
problems.ruling: Greek 'αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν' means they desire you (you emulate them), English reverses agency

problems.quote: I have been held worthy of the greatest honor
problems.why: Greek means ‘I considered it most valuable/excellent’, not that others have honored him.
problems.fix: I considered it most valuable
problems.ruling: ἠξίωμαι is passive 'I was deemed worthy/held worthy,' not active 'I considered.' μάλιστα πλείστης modifies the worthiness, not his valuation. Translator misread voice and syntax.

fixed: Changed 'do not want you to emulate them' to 'do not want you to be jealous of them' because ζηλοῦν means 'to be jealous/zealous', not 'to emulate'.

Changed 'it would have been unhindered for them to be emulated and for us to be imitated' to 'it was impossible for them to be jealous and to imitate us' because ἀκώλυτον means 'unhindered' but the context with ζηλοῦσθαι and μιμεῖσθαι indicates the opposite sense: it was impossible for them to be jealous and to imitate us.

Changed 'but rather they want to emulate you' to 'but that they themselves be emulated by you' because the Greek ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν means 'but themselves to emulate you' (i.e., they want you to emulate them), not 'they want to emulate you'.

Changed 'I have been held worthy of the greatest honor' to 'I considered it most valuable' because μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι means 'I considered it most valuable/excellent', not that others have honored him.

problems.quote: but that they themselves be emulated by you
problems.why: Greek says they themselves are jealous of you, not that they are to be emulated.
problems.fix: but that they themselves are jealous of you

problems.quote: make you emulated
problems.why: Greek says the actions make you jealous, not that they make you emulated.
problems.fix: make you jealous

problems.quote: and it was impossible for them to be jealous and to imitate us

problems.why: Modality flipped: 'it was unhindered/possible' not 'impossible'; misreads ἀκώλυτον.
problems.fix: and nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitating us
problems.ruling: ἀκώλυτον = unhindered, not impossible; modality reversed.

edits.new: but that they themselves are jealous of you

fixed: ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν means 'but they themselves are jealous of you', not 'be emulated by you'; edited.
ἃ καὶ ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ means 'which also make you jealous', not 'make you emulated'; edited.
ἀκώλυτον ἦν means 'it was unhindered', not 'impossible'; edited to 'nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitating us'.

problems.quote: those people do not want you to be jealous of them
problems.why: Greek says 'they want you not to be zealous/emulous', not 'do not want you to be jealous of them'.
problems.fix: those people want you not to be zealous
problems.ruling: Greek says ‘they want you not to be zealous’ (θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν), English adds ‘of them’ changing direction.

problems.quote: being emulated and imitating us
problems.why: Greek has 'to be emulated and to imitate us', not 'being emulated and imitating us' as parallel infinitives with same subject.
problems.fix: to be emulated and to imitate us
problems.ruling: Greek infinitives ζηλοῦσθαι (to be zealous) and μιμεῖσθαι (to imitate); English renders ζηλοῦσθαι as ‘being emulated’, wrong meaning.

problems.source_quote: τοιαῦτα πράττετε ἃ καὶ ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ
problems.why: Greek says 'do such things as also make you worthy of emulation/zealous', not 'make you jealous'.
problems.fix: do such things as make you worthy of emulation
problems.ruling: Greek phrase ‘… ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ’ means ‘makes you zealous’, not ‘make you jealous’.

fixed: Corrected 'do not want you to be jealous of them' to 'want you not to be zealous' per source 'θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν'.
Corrected 'being emulated and imitating us' to 'to be emulated and to imitate us' per source 'ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς'.
Corrected 'make you jealous' to 'make you worthy of emulation' per source 'ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ'.

problems.quote: works of the law
problems.why: Same concept rendered four ways; reader may miss they are equivalent.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'works of the law' or note equivalence.

problems.quote: basic principles
problems.why: Greek 'stoicheia'—could mean elemental spirits or elementary teachings; translation drifts between singular/plural and may confuse.
problems.fix: Add note explaining 'basic principles' = stoicheia, possibly spiritual powers.

problems.quote: Do not suppose, Paul says, that I had some other grievance
problems.why: Sudden shift to first-person as if Paul speaks directly; but context is Eusebius's commentary.
problems.fix: Use quotation marks or clarify 'Paul writes:'

problems.quote: For would that they also were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing hindered them from to be emulated and to imitate us.
problems.why: Ungrammatical: 'from to be emulated' is not English; missing noun or gerund.
problems.fix: Revise: 'and nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitated by us.'

problems.quote: Now he used the name, not the power, of allegory.
problems.why: Paradox is unclear without explanation of Eusebius's technical distinction.
problems.fix: Expand: 'He used the name "allegory" but not the literary device properly so called.'

problems.quote: What then is the blessing? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?
problems.why: 'It means: no one' makes no sense; likely a corrupted fragment or mistranslated gloss on Paul's text.
problems.fix: Check Greek; likely 'no one' is a misplaced marginal note or refers to 'no one can' do something.

problems.quote: nothing hindered them from to be emulated and to imitate us
problems.why: Ungrammatical English; 'from to be emulated' mixes infinitive and passive participle incorrectly.
problems.fix: Render as 'nothing hindered them from being worthy of emulation and imitating us.'

problems.quote: Do not suppose, Paul says, that I had some other grievance against you and for that reason I rebuke you.
problems.why: Unclear whether 'Paul says' introduces Paul's actual words or Eusebius's paraphrase of Paul's intent.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Eusebius explains: Paul is not rebuking them out of personal grievance.'

problems.quote: and in this way I helped them, and in this way I lead them captive to Babylon
problems.why: Shift from past ('helped') to present ('lead') in same clause is jarring; likely a tense confusion from the Greek.
problems.fix: Use consistent tense: 'and in this way I attached them to myself, and led them captive to Babylon.'

problems.quote: the basic principles
problems.why: Reader may not connect 'basic principles' (stoicheia) with the same concept in Galatians 4:9 and Colossians 2:8.
problems.fix: Add note: 'the basic principles (stoicheia)—the elemental spiritual powers behind law-observance.'

variants.text: the basic principles he worshiped when he was a Gentile

problems.quote: he did not accuse them as evil, but as unable to enrich and to suffice for piety
problems.why: 'to suffice for piety' is awkward English; likely means 'suffice for producing piety.'
problems.fix: Render as 'unable to enrich or to produce true piety.'

edits.old: For would that they also were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing hindered them from to be emulated and to imitate us.
edits.new: For would that they also were perfect, having made use of faith, and nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitating us.

edits.old: and in this way I helped them, and in this way I lead them captive to Babylon
edits.new: and in this way I helped them, and in this way I led them captive to Babylon

fixed: The glossary problems are not translation errors; the English uses the glossary terms correctly. No edit needed.
The speaker problem is not a translation error; the source has φησίν introducing Paul's words, and the English renders this naturally. No edit needed.
The 'from to be emulated' problem is real; the English is ungrammatical. Fixed to 'from being emulated and imitating us'.
The 'name, not the power, of allegory' problem is not a translation error; the English accurately renders the source's distinction between name and power. No edit needed.
The 'What then is the blessing? It means: no one' problem is not a translation error; the source has ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς, which the English renders correctly. No edit needed.
The 'nothing hindered them from to be emulated' problem is the same as the earlier ungrammatical problem; fixed.
The speaker problem is not a translation error; the source has φησίν, and the English renders it naturally. No edit needed.
The tense shift problem is real; the source has ἀπάγω (present) but the context is a past prophecy, and the English should be consistent. Fixed to 'led'.
The glossary problem is not a translation error; the English uses the glossary term correctly. No edit needed.
The 'to suffice for piety' problem is not a translation error; the English accurately renders the source's ἀρκεῖν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. No edit needed.

problems.quote: prophecy through deeds
problems.why: Same Greek concept rendered four ways; reader cannot see Eusebius's single technical category.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'prophecy enacted through deeds' throughout.

problems.quote: judaize
problems.why: Three renderings for same practice; 'keep the law' sounds positive, masking polemic.
problems.fix: Gloss 'judaize' on first use and use consistently.

problems.quote: For would that they also were perfect
problems.why: Unclear if Eusebius or Paul speaks; 'I say these things not envying them' blurs voices.
problems.fix: Mark as Eusebius explaining Paul's Gal 4:17-20.

problems.quote: What then is the blessing? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?
problems.why: Unintelligible without Greek; 'blessing' misrenders makarios ('blessed') as noun, and 'no one' is opaque.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'What then of the blessedness? Did it mean nothing? Or rather: is it law or faith?'

problems.quote: Behold, the virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14)
problems.why: Cited as 'prophecy through words alone' but Isaiah 7:14 includes sign-act context (7:10-11); Eusebius's category is strained.
problems.fix: Note: Eusebius isolates the verbal promise from its narrative setting.

problems.quote: Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9)
problems.why: Cited as 'deeds alone' but Numbers 21:8-9 includes God's verbal command; not pure deed.
problems.fix: Note: Eusebius emphasizes the enacted sign over accompanying words.

problems.quote: What then is the blessing? It means: no one.
problems.why: 'It means: no one' is nonsensical; the blessing cannot mean 'no one.'
problems.fix: Likely needs: 'What then is the blessing? No one [is blessed]—or is it by keeping the law or by faith?'

problems.quote: nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitating us
problems.why: Being emulated and imitating are opposite directions; one is passive, one active.
problems.fix: Likely: 'nothing hindered them from emulating and imitating us.'

problems.quote: Do not suppose, Paul says, that I had some other grievance against you
problems.why: Unclear if 'Paul says' introduces direct Scripture or Eusebius's paraphrase of Paul's intent.
problems.fix: Distinguish paraphrase from quotation consistently.

problems.quote: and in this way I helped them, and in this way I led them captive to Babylon
problems.why: 'Helped them' then 'led them captive' seems contradictory; likely a mistranslation of Jeremiah's waistcloth symbolism.
problems.fix: Check Greek: likely 'I adorned them' or 'I bound them to myself,' not 'helped.'

problems.quote: Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates.
problems.why: Jeremiah 13 says to buy a linen waistcloth, wear it, then go to the Euphrates to hide it—not 'take a new' one.
problems.fix: Cite as Jeremiah 13:1–4 and correct wording to match.

edits.new: What then is the blessedness? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?

edits.new: Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates (Jeremiah 13:1–4).

fixed: prophecy through deeds: The English uses 'prophecy through deeds' consistently in this section; no change needed.
judaize: The English does not use 'judaize' in this section; 'keeping the law' is the correct rendering of τηρεῖν νόμον.
For would that they also were perfect: The Greek ὤφελον γὰρ κἀκεῖνοι τέλειοι ἦσαν is Eusebius's own exclamation, not a quotation of Paul; the English is correct.

What then is the blessing? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?: The Greek μακαρισμός is a noun meaning 'blessedness' or 'blessing'; 'no one' is the answer to the question 'who is blessed?' The English is intelligible; changed 'blessing' to 'blessedness' for clarity.
Behold, the virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14): Eusebius cites this as a prophecy through words alone; the English correctly reflects his category.
Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9): Eusebius cites this as a prophecy through deeds alone; the English correctly reflects his category.
What then is the blessing? It means: no one.: The English is correct; 'no one' answers the implied question 'who is blessed?'

nothing hindered them from being emulated and imitating us: The Greek ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς means 'it was unhindered for them to be emulated and to imitate us'; the English 'being emulated and imitating us' is correct.
Do not suppose, Paul says, that I had some other grievance against you: The Greek φησίν introduces Paul's words; the English correctly marks the quotation.
and in this way I helped them, and in this way I led them captive to Babylon: The Greek περιεθέμην means 'I put on' (as a garment), not 'I helped'; corrected.
Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates.: The Greek λάβε περίζωμα καινὸν καὶ περίθου matches the English; added the citation.

problems.quote: the law
problems.why: Eusebius distinguishes 'commandments' (hearable, justifying) from 'works of the law' (bodily, toilsome), but this distinction is blurred by inconsistent rendering.
problems.fix: Clarify Eusebius's distinction between 'hearing commandments' and 'bodily works'.

problems.quote: basic principles
problems.why: Greek στοιχεῖα ('elements/basic principles') refers to elemental spirits or elementary teachings; 'basic principles' is opaque and its connection to law unclear.
problems.fix: Gloss as 'elemental spirits/powers' or explain equivalence to law.

problems.quote: The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin
problems.why: No indication who raises this question—Eusebius himself, an opponent, or a standard exegetical topos?
problems.fix: Add 'One might ask' or 'A question arises:'.

problems.quote: What then is the blessedness? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?
problems.why: Galatians 4:15 asks 'Where then is your blessedness?' (i.e., gratitude); 'It means: no one' is nonsensical as translation.
problems.fix: Correct to 'Where is your blessedness?' or 'What became of your blessedness?'

problems.quote: For there it is not a kiss, nor hair, nor belly, nor thighs, nor anything else
problems.why: Song of Songs 1:2 mentions only kisses; 'hair, belly, thighs' appear later in the book. Eusebius's 'there' seems to refer to allegory generally, not 1:2 specifically.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'In allegorical interpretation of the Song, it is not literally a kiss, hair, belly...'

problems.quote: Take a new waistcloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates (Jeremiah 13:1–4)
problems.why: Jeremiah 13:1-4 says 'Perath' (Euphrates in LXX), but the Hebrew likely means Parah near Jerusalem, not the distant Euphrates. Eusebius follows LXX, but the citation 'Jeremiah 13:1-4' is incomplete for his argument.
problems.fix: Extend citation to Jeremiah 13:1-11 or note LXX reading.

problems.quote: Do not suppose, Paul says, that I had some other grievance against you and for that reason I rebuke you.
problems.why: 'I' is Paul, but the sentence structure makes it seem like Eusebius is the one speaking in Paul's voice without clear quotation boundaries.
problems.fix: Use quotation marks: 'Paul says, "Do not suppose that I had some other grievance…"'

problems.quote: What then is the blessedness? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?
problems.why: Reader cannot tell whose question this is or what 'It means: no one' refers to.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Paul asks, What then is the blessedness? Eusebius explains: It refers to no one. Or rather: is it keeping the law or living by faith?'

problems.quote: And since he said that those people do not want to emulate you, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added: I say these things not envying them.
problems.why: Blends Eusebius's explanation with Paul's words ('he added: I say…') without clear quotation; 'those people' is unidentified.
problems.fix: Identify 'those people' as the circumcision party and mark Paul's words with quotes.

problems.quote: What then is the blessedness? It means: no one. Or this: is it keeping the law or living by faith?
problems.why: 'It means: no one' does not make sense in context; the sentence fragments are disconnected.
problems.fix: Reconstruct: 'What then is the blessedness? It belongs to no one. Or rather: is it keeping the law or living by faith?'

problems.quote: The passion of his pain constantly forces him to change the form of his speech
problems.why: 'Passion of his pain' is likely a literal rendering of a Greek phrase meaning 'the intensity of his anguish' or 'his deep pastoral concern.'
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'The depth of his anguish constantly forces him to change the form of his speech.'

fixed: The passion of his pain: re-read source; Greek ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος means 'the suffering of the pain,' but English 'passion of his pain' is awkward and misleading; changed to 'depth of his anguish' to convey intensity.

What then is the blessedness? It means: no one: source ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς means 'instead of: no one,' i.e., the blessedness belongs to no one; changed to 'It belongs to no one' and added 'rather' for clarity.
For there it is not a kiss: source refers to allegory in the Song of Songs generally, not just 1:2; clarified as 'in allegorical interpretation of the Song'.
Jeremiah citation: source quotes the waistcloth prophecy through the rotting and restoration, which extends beyond verse 4; extended citation to Jeremiah 13:1–11.
Do not suppose, Paul says: source φησίν introduces Paul's direct speech; added quotation marks to clarify speaker.
those people: source refers to Paul's opponents, the circumcision party; identified them explicitly and marked Paul's words with quotes.
Glossary 'the law': added gloss note distinguishing commandments from works of the law per Eusebius's argument.
Glossary 'basic principles': added gloss note explaining στοιχεῖα as elemental spirits or elementary teachings equivalent to the law.

fixed.quote: those people want you not to be zealous, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith without keeping the law, but that they themselves are jealous of you
fixed.fix: those people do not want to emulate you, so that they themselves may have the perfection of faith without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them
fixed.note: The contrast is 'they do not want to emulate you, but want you to emulate them'; the English garbles both halves, and the proposed fix is also wrong.

dismissed.quote: nothing hindered them from to be emulated and to imitate us
dismissed.why: Ungrammatical and wrong sense: ζηλοῦσθαι is passive 'to be emulated,' but the clause means 'it was unhindered for them to be emulated and to imitate us'—i.e., others could emulate them and they could imitate Paul.
dismissed.note: The quoted ungrammatical text is not in the English, which now reads 'nothing hindered them from emulating and imitating us'.

dismissed.quote: for I have been wronged in nothing by you
dismissed.why: Reverses agency: Paul says he has done no wrong to them, not that they have done nothing wrong to him.
dismissed.note: The passive παρ' ὑμῶν ἠδίκημαι means 'I have been wronged by you' (compare Galatians 4:12), so the English is right and the proposed fix reverses it.
